## The cost that turns up after signing

In most carve-outs, the seller's residual cost base is treated as a post-completion problem: something for the finance team to work through once the deal has closed. That is too late. By then the price is fixed, the TSA fees are agreed and the separation plan is set.

Stranded cost is the part of the seller's cost base that supported the divested business and does not leave with it. It shapes the economics of the deal for both sides. Treating it as a diligence question, sized before terms are settled, changes what a seller accepts and what a buyer pays.

## Where it comes from in financial services carve-outs

Financial services groups run on shared platforms and shared control functions. When a business leaves, its share of those costs does not disappear on completion day.

| Source | Why it strands |
| --- | --- |
| Technology licences and infrastructure | Enterprise licences and data centre capacity are priced on group volumes and cannot be cut in proportion |
| Control functions | Risk, compliance, audit, finance and legal are sized for the group; regulatory obligations do not shrink with revenue |
| Property | Floors and sites were shared; leases run on |
| Shared operations | Contact centres, payments and back-office teams lose volume but keep fixed overhead |
| Vendor contracts | Minimum commitments and volume tiers were negotiated for the whole group |
| TSA delivery | Staff and systems kept to deliver TSAs can only be removed when the TSAs exit, and only if exit is planned |

The last row is the one sellers control most directly. A TSA priced at cost-plus recovers cost while it runs. When it ends, the cost is still there unless the seller has a plan to remove it on the same timetable.

## Why it belongs in price and deal terms

For a seller, stranded cost is part of the real proceeds of a sale. A headline price that looks attractive can be worth much less once the residual cost base is counted, and boards should see both numbers together when they decide.

It also affects the negotiating position on terms that are usually settled quickly:

- **TSA pricing.** If cost-plus does not cover the cost the seller must carry to deliver services, the seller is subsidising the buyer for the life of the TSA.
- **TSA duration and extensions.** Every extension delays the seller's cost-out. Extension pricing should step up to reflect that.
- **Exit obligations.** Firm exit dates, with the buyer carrying the cost of late exit, protect the seller's cost-out plan.
- **Reverse TSAs.** Services the seller still needs from the divested business create cost the seller does not control.

None of these can be negotiated well without a sized view of what strands and when it can be removed.

## How to size it in two weeks

A useful estimate does not need a full cost allocation study. It needs the right people and a clear method.

1. **Start from the allocation, not the ledger.** Take the cost allocated to the divested business in management accounts and split it into direct cost (leaves with the business) and allocated cost (stays behind).
2. **Test each allocated line for variability.** For each, ask what share can be removed within twelve months of TSA exit, and what action it takes: contract renegotiation, headcount reduction, site consolidation, platform decommissioning.
3. **Map against the TSA schedule.** Cost that supports TSA services cannot be removed until those services exit. Align the cost-out timeline to the TSA exit plan.
4. **Separate one-off from run-rate.** Decommissioning, redundancy and contract exit costs are one-off. What remains after them is the true stranded run-rate.
5. **Put a range on it.** A low and high estimate, with the main assumptions stated, is enough to inform price and terms.

The output should fit on one page for the board: stranded run-rate, one-off cost to remove it, the timetable, and the deal terms that protect it.

## The buyer's side of the same problem

The mirror of the seller's stranded cost is the buyer's standalone cost: what the business will cost to run once it no longer has the parent's scale. Information memoranda tend to present a carve-out on its historical allocated cost. That number rarely survives contact with standalone vendor pricing, a separate control function and a new technology estate.

Buyers that size standalone cost in diligence, and test it against the TSA scope, avoid paying for synergies that turn into dis-synergies. Private equity buyers in particular, without a parent of their own to absorb the business, should treat it as a core valuation input.

On both sides, the work is the same: understand what the business really depends on, and what it will cost when that dependency ends. Doing it before signing is cheaper than finding out afterwards.
